Post 001 · October 21, 2026

The Ship That Never Left the Dock

The SS Eastland disaster. Chicago, July 24, 1915. A ship that never left the wharf, and the 844 people who died anyway.

Disasters 6 images 4:5 · 1080×1350 Viral score 37/40
View the post Season calendar

The story

844 people died on a ship that never went anywhere.

On the morning of July 24, 1915, the excursion steamer Eastland was moored on the Chicago River, loading Western Electric employees and their families for a company picnic. More than 2,500 people came aboard. The gangplank was still down.

Shortly after 7 a.m., the ship rolled onto its side. The river there is about twenty feet deep, and the hull came to rest about twenty feet from the wharf. That shallow, narrow gap is why hundreds climbed out alive — and why hundreds below deck had minutes, not hours.

844 passengers and crew died. 590 were under 25. Twenty-two entire families were wiped out. A grand jury indicted the owners, the captain, the chief engineer, and federal inspectors. The cases ended without a conviction.

The record

What the fact-check changed.

Gate 2 exists because research drifts. In this post it caught two material errors before a single caption was written.

  • A fabricated defendant. The draft named a man who does not appear in any source connected to the case. Removed.
  • A false conviction claim. The widely repeated story that the chief engineer was convicted conflates a 1933 civil ruling with criminal guilt. The defendants were acquitted in February 1916 and no trial was ever held in Chicago. Corrected.

An unsupported death-toll figure was also removed, and the rights audit caught a wrong Library of Congress identifier written from memory. The full trail is in the process record.

The Ship That Never Left the Dock

The SS Eastland, Chicago, July 24, 1915. Six archival frames, in order.

Carousel · 6 frames · click any image to enlarge

Instagram caption

Platform copy

The Eastland was still tied to the dock when it killed 844 people.

Chicago, July 24, 1915. Shortly after 7 a.m., employees of Western Electric and their families boarded a five-deck excursion steamer bound for a company picnic in Michigan City, Indiana. More than 2,500 people were on board. The gangplank was still down. The ship had not gone anywhere.

It had almost gone over before. In 1904 it nearly capsized with roughly 3,000 people aboard. In 1912 it listed hard in Cleveland. Narrow, fast, and top-heavy, the Eastland had a stability problem its operators knew about.

Then came a reform meant to make ships safer. After the Titanic sank, a 1915 federal law required more lifeboats. To keep its passenger license, the Eastland added boats high on its upper decks. The weight went exactly where the ship could least afford it.

Shortly after 7 a.m., the Eastland lurched and rolled onto its side.

The river there is about 20 feet deep, and the ship came to rest about 20 feet from the wharf. That shallow, narrow gap is why hundreds climbed across the exposed hull and lived — and why hundreds below deck had minutes, not hours.

844 passengers and crew died. 590 were under 25. Twenty-two entire families were wiped out.

A grand jury indicted the owners, the captain, the chief engineer, and federal inspectors. The cases ended without a conviction.

The Eastland was raised weeks later, sold, and eventually commissioned as the Navy's USS Wilmette. She served until 1945 and was scrapped in 1947.

The dock is a short walk from the Loop. The water is 20 feet deep. Most days, nobody looks down.

Photographs: National Archives and Records Administration; Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division.

#EastlandDisaster #ChicagoHistory #GreatLakes #MaritimeHistory #ForgottenHistory

Facebook caption

The same story, told for Facebook

On the morning of July 24, 1915, the Eastland was still tied to the dock when it rolled onto its side and killed 844 people.

The Eastland was an excursion steamer. That Saturday it was carrying employees of Western Electric and their families to a company picnic in Michigan City, Indiana. More than 2,500 people came aboard. The gangplank was still down.

The ship had a history. It nearly capsized at its dock in 1904 with about 3,000 people aboard, and it listed severely in Cleveland in 1912. Fast and narrow, the Eastland was top-heavy. The people who ran it knew it had stability problems.

Then a safety reform made those problems worse. After the Titanic sank, a 1915 federal law required more lifeboats. To keep its licensed passenger capacity, the Eastland's operators added lifeboats and rafts high on the upper decks. All that weight sat above the ship's center of gravity.

Shortly after 7 a.m., the Eastland lurched to port and rolled onto its side.

Here is the part that is hard to hold in your head. The ship did not sink. The Chicago River is only about 20 feet deep there, and the hull came to rest about 20 feet from the wharf. Hundreds of people climbed across the exposed side of the ship to the dock and lived.

Hundreds of others were below decks, in the cabins and the dance floor, when the water came in. They had minutes.

844 passengers and crew died, including 590 people under the age of 25. Twenty-two families lost every member.

A grand jury indicted the ship's owners, captain, chief engineer, and federal inspectors. The case was moved to Michigan, where the defendants were found not guilty in February 1916, and the court refused extradition back to Illinois. No criminal trial was ever held in Chicago. No one was convicted.

The Eastland was raised on August 14, 1915. She was sold, and in 1918 she was commissioned as the U.S. Navy's USS Wilmette, serving until 1945 before being scrapped.

The site is a few blocks from the Loop, on a stretch of river where tour boats now run. The water is 20 feet deep. Most days, nobody looks down.

Photographs: National Archives and Records Administration; Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division.

#EastlandDisaster #ChicagoHistory #MaritimeHistory #GreatLakes

01 — Cover

A long passenger steamship lies completely on its side in a narrow city river, its dark hull exposed above the waterline. A few small figures stand on the upturned hull, and brick warehouses line the shore.

02 — The ship

A tall white excursion steamship with two funnels and several decks sits upright at a city dock, seen bow-on so its full height fills the frame.

03 — The moment

A dramatic black-and-white newspaper drawing shows a large steamship tilting sharply toward the water as tiny figures scramble on its decks and swim below, watched from a bridge.

04 — The hull

A huge dark hull fills the frame at water level, seen from a boat on the river. The overturned steamship's curved side rises above the water beside a stone river wall.

05 — The rescue

Dozens of people stand on the exposed side of a capsized steamship while small rowboats and launches crowd the water around it. A dense crowd watches from the riverbank.

06 — The wreck

A wide sepia photograph shows a city river crowded with boats and onlookers, with the exposed hull of a capsized steamship beside a bridge and tall warehouses.

Briefs

What each post is for

A brief is not a script. It is a reason to spend research time, plus the specific questions that research has to answer.

Post 001 · Disasters / Engineering failure

The Ship That Never Left the Dock

Wednesday, Oct 21, 2026 · provisional score 37/40 · ready

A steamship capsized while still secured to its dock, killing 844 people in twenty feet of water, twenty feet from shore.

Why it earns a slot
The strongest single story in the slate: an impossible fact in one sentence, real engineering substance, and an abundant free visual archive.
Sources to verify
U.S. National Archives (NAID 281840, 281841); Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division; H.Res. 375, 114th Congress; Eastland Disaster Historical Society
Imagery outlook
Excellent. Six authentic public-domain frames; renderer complete.
Risks
None outstanding. Two common false claims (an 812 toll and an engineer's conviction) were removed at Gate 2.

Post 002 · Disasters

The Fire That Was Forgotten

Wednesday, Oct 28, 2026 · provisional score 36/40 · planned

On the same night Chicago burned, a wildfire in Wisconsin killed an estimated 1,500 to 2,500 people — the deadliest in American history — and almost nobody remembers it.

Why it earns a slot
The Chicago comparison is a built-in hook and a genuine historical injustice. It is the purest 'I never knew this' story on the slate.
Sources to verify
Wisconsin Historical Society; National Weather Service historical records; Peshtigo Fire Museum; Contemporary Wisconsin and Chicago newspapers, 1871
Imagery outlook
Weak. Surviving photographs are scarce; expect period engravings and later commemorative images. May justify a documentary-style reconstruction with full disclosure, or a text-forward plate design.
Risks
Death toll is an estimate and ranges widely by source. Must be presented as an estimate, never a precise figure. Low photographic record is the main production risk.

Post 003 · Engineering failure

The Dam Nobody Would Fix

Wednesday, Nov 4, 2026 · provisional score 37/40 · planned

A private club's earthen dam failed above Johnstown, Pennsylvania, and killed 2,209 people. The club's members included some of the richest men in America.

Why it earns a slot
Class, negligence, and documented warnings ignored. The clearest accountability story available, and the imagery is strong.
Sources to verify
Johnstown Flood Museum; National Park Service; American Society of Civil Engineers; Contemporary Pennsylvania press, 1889
Imagery outlook
Strong. Widely held period photographs, public domain.
Risks
The club's responsibility is well documented but the legal outcome needs precision. Avoid turning it into a simple morality play.

Post 004 · Disasters / Safety

The Doors That Opened Inward

Wednesday, Nov 11, 2026 · provisional score 37/40 · planned

A Chicago theater fire killed 602 people in about fifteen minutes. Many of the exits were locked, blocked, or opened inward.

Why it earns a slot
A direct safety-failure story with a physical mechanism a reader can picture, and Chicago continuity with Post 001.
Sources to verify
Chicago History Museum; National Fire Protection Association historical records; Cook County coroner's inquest, 1903; Contemporary Chicago press
Imagery outlook
Strong. Period photographs, postcards, and architectural images.
Risks
Graphic subject. No imagery of victims. Verify each specific exit failure before naming it.

Post 005 · Labor / Disasters

The Worst Mining Disaster in American History

Wednesday, Nov 18, 2026 · provisional score 35/40 · planned

An explosion in a West Virginia mine killed at least 362 men and boys. It led directly to the creation of the federal Bureau of Mines.

Why it earns a slot
Labor history with a concrete policy consequence, and a death toll that is still argued over.
Sources to verify
Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA); West Virginia State Archives; U.S. Bureau of Mines records; Contemporary West Virginia press
Imagery outlook
Moderate. Period photographs exist; some are graphic and must be excluded.
Risks
Death toll varies from 362 to over 500 depending on the source. Child labor is central and needs care. Dignity review required.

Post 006 · Disasters

The Blast That Flattened a City

Tuesday, Nov 24, 2026 · provisional score 37/40 · planned

Two ships collided in Halifax harbor and the munitions cargo detonated, killing about 2,000 people and injuring thousands more.

Post 007 · Engineering failure

The Wave That Came From a Tank

Wednesday, Dec 2, 2026 · provisional score 36/40 · planned

A storage tank in Boston's North End burst and sent a wall of molasses through the streets, killing 21 people.

Why it earns a slot
The hook is irresistible and the underlying failure — a tank built too thin, never properly tested — is genuinely instructive.
Sources to verify
Boston Public Library; Boston Globe archives, 1919; National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration; Engineering case studies
Imagery outlook
Strong. Period photographs widely held.
Risks
Tone is the whole risk. It reads as trivia if handled lightly. Verify the claimed wave speed and the toll.

Post 008 · Labor / Science

The Women Who Glowed

Wednesday, Dec 9, 2026 · provisional score 36/40 · planned

Factory workers painted watch dials with radium and were told it was safe. Their bodies became the evidence that changed American labor law.

Why it earns a slot
Human, scientific, and legally consequential. It broadens the season beyond disasters into science and labor.
Sources to verify
Argonne National Laboratory; Occupational Safety and Health Administration; Illinois and New Jersey state archives; Federal court records
Imagery outlook
Moderate. Portraits are limited and rights vary by item. Some medical imagery must be excluded.
Risks
Portrait rights need per-item verification. Avoid lurid medical detail. Verify names, dates, and the legal outcomes.

Post 009 · Disasters / Medicine

The Fire That Changed Burn Care

Wednesday, Dec 16, 2026 · provisional score 35/40 · planned

A Boston nightclub fire killed 492 people. The treatment of its survivors produced the first modern burn protocol.

Why it earns a slot
Held from the Post 001 shortlist. A double payoff: the disaster and the medical legacy that came out of it.
Sources to verify
Boston Public Library; Massachusetts General Hospital archives; National Fire Protection Association; Contemporary Boston press
Imagery outlook
Moderate. Period exterior photographs exist; interiors are scarce.
Risks
Graphic subject; no victim imagery. Verify the toll and the specific medical claims, which are often overstated.

Post 010 · Disasters / Safety

The Tent That Burned in Minutes

Wednesday, Jan 6, 2027 · provisional score 36/40 · planned

A circus tent treated with paraffin and gasoline caught fire during a matinee in Hartford, killing 167 people, most of them children.

Why it earns a slot
Devastating and largely forgotten, with a clear materials-failure mechanism and a direct line to modern flame-retardant rules.
Sources to verify
Connecticut Historical Society; National Fire Protection Association; Hartford Circus Fire memorial records; Contemporary Hartford press
Imagery outlook
Moderate. Period photographs exist and require careful selection.
Risks
The highest emotional content on the slate, involving children. Dignity review is mandatory. Verify the tent treatment claim precisely.

Provisional scores are estimates made before research. Every claim in a brief must pass the same Gate 2 audit that Post 001 did, and any of these can be killed at Gate 1 if the sources do not hold up.

The operating manual

How the studio works.

Eighteen roles, eleven stages, six gates, and one rule that matters more than the rest: nothing moves forward on vibes.

Cluefolio Studio — Agency Operating Manual

Version 1.0 · Owner: agency-lead · Read this before any assignment.

Cluefolio Studio is a small, evidence-first storytelling agency. We produce research-backed, image-led stories about real events for Instagram and Facebook, primarily for a US audience.

We are not a content farm. We do not rewrite viral posts. We do not invent detail. We do not publish a story we cannot defend line by line.

1. The promise

Every post must satisfy four conditions before it leaves the building:

  1. It is true. Every material claim traces to a source a skeptic could open.
  2. It is original. The angle, structure, and language are ours, not a paraphrase of someone else's post.
  3. It earns its length. Every paragraph and every image adds information, context, or feeling.
  4. It pays off. The reader who finishes gets an answer, a meaning, or an honest unresolved question.

If any condition fails, the post does not ship. A missed week is cheaper than a correction.

Gate rules

  • G1 Greenlight — the story is strong enough to spend research time on. editorial-director decides.
  • G2 Factual lock — every claim is VERIFIED, DISPUTED, or UNSUPPORTED. Writing cannot start until

every load-bearing claim is VERIFIED and every DISPUTED claim has approved handling language.

  • G3 Rights clearance — every image has a license, a source URL, and a credit line. standards-editor signs off.
  • G4 Story approval — the outline has a hook, a turn, and a payoff. editorial-director decides.
  • G5 Clearance — dignity, disclosure, policy, accessibility. standards-editor can veto.
  • G6 Sign-off — automated checks pass and every asset was visually inspected. qa-lead decides.

A gate failure returns the work to the owning agent with a written reason. Maximum three revision rounds per gate, then the post is either fixed or killed.

4. Claim IDs

Every verified fact gets an ID in 03-source-ledger.md:

C01 | 844 passengers and crew died | VERIFIED | NARA + Congress + EDHS
C02 | The ship capsized while still tied to the dock | VERIFIED | Board of inquiry testimony

Captions must be traceable to these IDs. In post-metadata.json, list the claim IDs each caption relies on. This is how we stop a beautiful story from drifting off the facts.

5. The Viral Readiness Score

"Viral" is not a promise. It is a set of controllable inputs. Score every post 1–5 on eight criteria:

CriterionQuestion
HookDoes the first line stop a scroll in under 3 seconds?
Curiosity gapIs there a real question the story actually answers?
Emotional stakesAwe, grief, injustice, wonder — is it felt?
SpecificityNames, numbers, dates, places?
Visual stopping powerDoes image 1 work at thumbnail size?
Shareability"I didn't know this" or "you have to see this"?
SaveabilityIs the payoff worth keeping?
Comment potentialIs there an honest open question, not rage bait?

40 points max. Publish at ≥32. Flagship at ≥36.

Record the score in post-metadata.json and justify each number in one line.

6. Operating rules

Orchestration

Subagents cannot spawn subagents in this environment. agency-lead launches every specialist directly, in parallel where safe. Use the minimum number of agents that improves quality.

Fresh context

Every brief is self-contained: absolute paths, the artifact to produce, the template, acceptance criteria, and the relevant brand file. Never assume a subagent remembers a previous conversation.

One artifact per agent

No two agents write the same file. This keeps parallel work mergeable.

Handoff block

Every agent ends its output with:

HANDOFF
status: PASS | FAIL | BLOCKED
changed: <files written>
open: <unresolved questions>
next: <agent id>

Cost and safety

  • Free models only. No paid API usage, ever, without written authorization.
  • No subscriptions, no credits, no purchases.
  • No credentials in files, logs, or captions.
  • No posting, messaging, or publishing. We deliver a package; a human publishes it.
  • Never upload private project data to a third party.
  • Inspect unfamiliar scripts before running them.

Research ethics

Respect robots policies, rate limits, platform terms, copyright, and privacy. Do not bypass authentication, paywalls, CAPTCHAs, or access controls. Do not scrape logged-in social platforms without authorization. Public archive APIs with documented terms are fair game.

7. Editorial standards

We publish

  • Verified facts, attributed clearly.
  • Disputed accounts labeled as disputed, with the competing versions named.
  • Public-domain or properly licensed imagery with credits.
  • AI reconstructions only when authentic imagery is unavailable, always disclosed.
  • Honest unresolved endings when the record genuinely has no answer.

We refuse

  • Fabricated quotes, scenes, documents, or statistics.
  • AI imagery presented as documentary evidence.
  • Graphic death imagery used for shock.
  • Naming private individuals in a damaging light without public-interest justification.
  • Engagement bait, fake urgency, "you won't believe," and withheld essential facts.
  • Copying another creator's distinctive wording or structure.
  • Speculation dressed as fact.

Victim dignity

Disasters involve real families. We describe scale and consequence without lingering on corpses, identifiable remains, or gratuitous suffering. When in doubt, choose the frame that respects the dead.

8. Voice

Plainspoken, cinematic, evidence-first.

  • Specific over dramatic. "844 people died 20 feet from shore" beats "a tragedy beyond imagination."
  • Short paragraphs. One idea each. Mobile-first.
  • No purple prose, no adjective stacking, no rhetorical questions as filler.
  • American English. Contractions are fine.
  • The reader should feel trusted, not manipulated.

See brand/voice.md for the full guide and worked examples.

10. Definition of done

A post is done when:

  • [ ] Story selected, angle stated in one sentence.
  • [ ] Every load-bearing claim VERIFIED and traceable.
  • [ ] Disputed points handled explicitly.
  • [ ] Every image has a license, source, credit, and provenance record.
  • [ ] Every final image inspected at full size.
  • [ ] Captions complete for both platforms, platform-native.
  • [ ] Alt text written for every image.
  • [ ] Viral Readiness Score ≥32, with justification.
  • [ ] Standards clearance passed.
  • [ ] Automated validation passed.
  • [ ] Paths in the final report actually exist.

Brand system

Voice, look, and refusals.

What we sound like, what we look like, and what we will not publish.

Cluefolio Voice

The one-line version

We tell true stories the way a good documentary does: calmly, specifically, and with respect for the people involved.

Principles

1. Specificity is the drama

Weak: "It was a tragedy beyond imagination." Strong: "The water was twenty feet deep. The dock was twenty feet away."

Numbers, names, dates, and physical details do the emotional work. Adjectives do not.

2. Trust the reader

We never say "you won't believe," "what happened next shocked everyone," or "wait for it." We give the reader the facts in the best order and let them feel it.

3. One idea per paragraph

Mobile reading is vertical and impatient. A paragraph is one beat. Two to four sentences. White space is part of the design.

4. Calm authority

No exclamation marks. No all-caps for emphasis. No emoji unless it carries real meaning (we generally avoid them in captions; a single arrow or map pin is acceptable).

5. Respect the dead

Describe scale and consequence without lingering. Do not aestheticize suffering. Do not use a death toll as a punchline or a hook gimmick.

6. Original phrasing

We do not lift sentences, structures, or signature moves from other creators. If a phrase feels borrowed, rewrite it.

7. End with weight

The last line should land. It can be a fact, a turn, a quiet image, or an honest question. It should never be a call to "follow for more."

Sentence rhythm

Vary length deliberately. A long, detailed sentence followed by a short one creates emphasis.

The ship had been built for speed, modified for capacity, and inspected for everything except the one thing that would kill it. Stability.

Openings we use

  • A concrete image: "At 7:28 on a July morning, a 265-foot steamship rolled onto its side in the Chicago River."
  • A contradiction: "The ship never left the dock. That is the part people forget."
  • A number with a physical anchor: "844 people died in twenty feet of water."

Openings we ban

  • "In [year], something happened that would change everything."
  • "Imagine you are..."
  • "This is the story of..."
  • "You've probably never heard of..."
  • "What happened next will..."

Words we avoid

journey, unbelievable, shocking, chilling, haunting, tragic (as a crutch), iconic, legendary, "little did they know," "forever changed," "in a matter of minutes" (unless precise).

Words we like

still, tied, dock, hull, ballast, list, roll, manifest, inquiry, verdict, ledger, unclaimed.

InstagramFacebook
LengthTighter, ~1,200–1,800 charsCan run longer, ~1,800–2,600 chars
Line breaksFrequent, generousSlightly denser, still short paragraphs
Hashtags4–6 at the end3–4, or none
First lineMust work above the "more" foldMust work in the feed preview
ToneSlightly more visual, immediateSlightly more explanatory, narrative

Both must tell the same factual story. Neither is a copy of the other.

Cluefolio Visual Identity

The idea

An archival research desk, not a tabloid. Warm paper, dark ink, restrained type, and photographs that are allowed to be photographs.

The grid should be recognizable before anyone reads the wordmark.

Canvas

  • Primary: 1080 × 1350 (4:5 portrait) — Instagram and Facebook feed.
  • Secondary: 1080 × 1080 (1:1) — only if a platform crop demands it.
  • Story/Reel cover: 1080 × 1920 — future use, not part of Post 001.
  • Color profile: sRGB. Format: JPEG, quality 92, progressive.
  • Max file size: 8 MB per image (Instagram feed limit is generous; stay well under).

Palette

RoleHexUse
Paper#F4EFE6Background, caption panels
Ink#15130FHeadlines, body text
Muted ink#5B5348Secondary text, credits
Rule#B9AE9CHairlines, dividers
Accent#8C2F1ECategory tag, key numerals
Deep shadow#0B0A08Vignette, overlay scrim

Never use pure white #FFFFFF for type on paper. Never use pure black #000000 for text.

Typography

  • Display: Georgia Bold — headlines, numerals.
  • Secondary display: Georgia Italic — pull quotes, datelines.
  • Text: Segoe UI — captions, credits, labels.
  • Labels: Segoe UI Semibold, letter-spaced 0.14em, uppercase, 22–26 px.

Rules:

  • Headline max 2 lines on the cover, max 3 on interior.
  • Never stretch or condense type. Never outline it.
  • Minimum body size on-image: 28 px at 1080 wide.
  • Minimum credit size: 20 px.

Cover lockup (image 01)

Fixed positions, identical on every post:

┌──────────────────────────────┐
│  CLUEFOLIO        [CATEGORY] │  ← top rail, 72 px from edges
│                              │
│                              │
│         [photograph]         │
│                              │
│                              │
│  THE SHIP THAT               │  ← headline, Georgia Bold
│  NEVER LEFT THE DOCK         │
│  ────────────────            │  ← 3 px accent rule
│  Chicago, July 24, 1915      │  ← dateline, Georgia Italic
└──────────────────────────────┘
  • Top rail: wordmark left, category tag right, both in muted ink.
  • Headline sits in the lower third, on a soft gradient scrim for legibility.
  • Accent rule is 120 px wide, 3 px tall.
  • Never place the headline over a busy area without a scrim.

Interior pages (02–06)

  • Full-bleed photograph, slight warm grade, subtle grain.
  • A 40 px paper-colored margin is not used; images bleed to the edge.
  • A bottom credit strip: 96 px tall, paper background, 90% opacity, muted ink text.
  • Optional short caption line above the credit strip (max 90 characters) in Georgia Italic.
  • Page number bottom-right in Segoe UI, muted ink.

Image treatment

  • Grade: warm highlights, slightly lifted blacks, desaturated by 8–12%. Never crush detail.
  • Grain: subtle, 2–4% opacity. Enough to unify scans of different quality.
  • Sharpening: light unsharp mask after resize. Never over-sharpen archival scans.
  • Cropping: crop for composition, never to distort. Never upscale beyond 1.6× original.
  • No fake colorization. If an image is black and white, it stays black and white.
  • No AI fills, no generative expand, no invented detail.

Consistency across a carousel

  • Same palette, same type, same credit strip position on every image.
  • Image 1 is the only one with the headline lockup.
  • Images 2–6 carry a small category tag in the top-left so a screenshot is still identifiable.

Alt text

Every image gets alt text written for a screen-reader user, not for SEO. Describe what is visible and what it shows, in one to three sentences. Do not begin with "Image of."

Example:

A long passenger steamship lies completely on its side in a narrow city river, its hull exposed above the waterline. Small boats cluster alongside, and a few figures stand on the upturned hull.

Accessibility

  • No essential information conveyed only by color.

Publishing checklist

  • [ ] Images exported at 1080 × 1350, sRGB, JPEG q92.
  • [ ] Carousel order matches 08-visual-plan.md.
  • [ ] Caption within platform limit.
  • [ ] Hashtags specific and relevant.

  • [ ] AI disclosure included if any generated imagery is used.
  • [ ] Scheduled or posted manually by a human.

Hook Rubric

The hook is the first line of the caption and the first frame of the carousel. It has one job: make a specific promise the story keeps.

The three-second test

A scrolling user sees roughly 125 characters and one image. In three seconds they decide.

Ask:

  1. Is there a concrete noun or number in the first six words?
  2. Is there a contradiction, a stake, or an unanswered question?
  3. Does it avoid every banned opening in voice.md?
  4. Does the image add a second, non-redundant piece of information?

Hook patterns that work for us

The impossible fact

The ship never left the dock.

The number with a physical anchor

844 people died in twenty feet of water, twenty feet from shore.

The contradiction

A brand-new safety law helped kill 844 people.

The quiet image

At 7:28 on a July morning, a 265-foot steamship rolled onto its side in downtown Chicago.

The delayed consequence

The captain survived. He was one of the last people to walk off his own ship.

Scoring a hook (1–5 each)

Dimension135
SpecificityVagueSome detailConcrete noun + number + place
TensionNoneMild curiosityGenuine unanswered question
Payoff honestyOverpromisesRoughly fairExactly what the story delivers
Visual pairingImage repeats textImage supports textImage and text add different information
Voice fitGenericAcceptableUnmistakably Cluefolio

20 max. Ship at ≥16. Below 16, rewrite, do not ship.

What we never do

  • Withhold the death toll to force a click.
  • Use "you won't believe" or "wait for it."
  • Promise a mystery the story resolves in the first paragraph.
  • Put a question mark where a fact belongs.
  • Use a corpse or a grieving face as the thumbnail.

Worked example

Weak: "This forgotten disaster shocked Chicago. 🧵"

Why: vague, no specifics, engagement bait, emoji as decoration.

Better: "844 people died on a ship that never left the dock."

Why: number, contradiction, honest.

Best: "The ship never left the dock. 844 people died anyway."

Why: two short sentences, a real contradiction, and the image supplies the ship.

Editorial Standards & Refusals

Binding on every agent. standards-editor enforces at Gate 5 and holds veto power.

1. Truth

  • Every material claim must trace to a source in 03-source-ledger.md.
  • Direct quotations must come from a primary source or a reputable secondary source that quotes it.

If we cannot verify the exact wording, we paraphrase without quotation marks.

  • Numbers must match a cited source. When sources disagree, we say so.
  • Causal claims ("X caused Y") require a source that actually asserts causation, not our inference.
  • We distinguish what happened, what a court found, and what historians argue.

2. Originality

  • We do not copy sentences, paragraph structures, or signature phrases from other creators.
  • We may use facts from any reputable source; we write them ourselves.
  • We do not present a Wikipedia article, lightly edited, as reporting.
  • If our angle is common, we must add verified depth that the common version lacks.

3. Imagery

  • Authentic first. Public-domain archives, government collections, museum open-access, or

properly licensed stock.

  • Verify the image belongs to the story. A file named "Eastland" is not proof. Check the

catalog record, date, and creator.

  • Rights: record the license, the source URL, and the credit line. "Found on Google" is not a license.
  • AI reconstructions are permitted only when authentic imagery is unavailable or unusable, and

must be disclosed in the caption and in post-metadata.json.

  • Never present an AI image as a historical photograph. Never add generated detail to a real

archival image.

  • No generative fill, no AI upscaling that invents texture, no synthetic faces on real people.

4. Dignity

  • Disasters involve identifiable families. We describe scale and consequence without lingering on

corpses, remains, or recognizable suffering.

  • We do not use death imagery as a thumbnail.
  • We do not name private individuals in a damaging light absent a clear public interest.
  • Victims are people, not set dressing. Where we can, we name them accurately and with care.

5. Platform policy

  • No graphic violence or gore in feed images.
  • No harassment, hate, or targeted negativity.
  • No medical or legal advice.
  • No misleading health, safety, or financial claims.
  • Disclose AI-generated imagery where platforms require it, and where viewers could be misled.
  • Respect copyright and attribution requirements.

6. Engagement ethics

We do not:

  • Ask a question we do not answer to farm comments.
  • Use rage bait, tribalism, or manufactured controversy.
  • Withhold the resolution to inflate watch time.
  • Post the same caption to every platform.
  • Buy or trade engagement.

We do:

  • End with a genuine open question when the record is genuinely open.
  • Invite correction and respond to it honestly.
  • Credit archives and researchers.

7. Corrections

If a published post contains a material error:

  1. Correct the caption or image within 24 hours.
  2. Add a visible correction note in the caption or first comment.
  3. Log it in the post's 14-postmortem.md.
  4. If the error is structural, unpublish and rebuild.

We do not silently edit and pretend it did not happen.

8. AI disclosure language

When used, disclose plainly in the caption:

Some images in this post are AI-generated reconstructions, not historical photographs. They are labeled in the caption.

And label the specific image:

Image 4: AI reconstruction, not a photograph.

Never bury the disclosure in hashtags.

Production Brief — The Ship That Never Left the Dock

Slug: first-post

Category: Disasters / Engineering failure

Date: 2026-10-19

Owner: agency-lead

Stage: 0 — Brief

Status: APPROVED

1. The assignment

One complete, publication-ready image-led post for Instagram and Facebook, aimed at a US audience. No monthly calendar. This is Post 001 and it must establish the studio's standard.

2. The angle

A steamship capsized while still tied to its dock, killing 844 people in twenty feet of water, twenty feet from shore — and nobody was ever held responsible.

3. Why this story, why now

  • The central fact is a contradiction strong enough to stop a scroll: the ship never left the dock.
  • It is a genuine engineering-failure story: top-weight, stability, and a safety law that made a

known flaw worse. That makes it relevant to modern readers, not just history buffs.

  • Primary sources are abundant and free: NARA, the Library of Congress, congressional records.
  • It is widely under-known relative to its scale — 844 deaths, the deadliest wreck in Great Lakes

history — which gives it "I never knew this" share value.

  • Authentic public-domain photography exists, so no AI reconstruction is needed and no disclosure

is required.

4. Non-negotiable facts

These are verified before writing and may not change without a new fact-check:

  • The Eastland capsized on July 24, 1915, in the Chicago River, while still moored to the wharf.
  • 844 passengers and crew died.
  • The water at the site was about 20 feet deep; the ship lay roughly 20 feet from the dock wall.
  • The ship had a documented history of severe listing before the disaster.
  • The dead included a large number of young people and multiple entire families.
  • Criminal prosecutions ended without a conviction.
  • The ship was later raised, renamed USS Wilmette, and served into the 1940s.

5. Audience

US adults 25–55 who follow history, engineering failures, and true-story accounts on Instagram and Facebook. They save and share posts that teach them something specific they did not know. They dislike being manipulated and they notice errors.

6. Platforms and format

  • Instagram: 4:5, 1080×1350, caption ≤2,200 characters, 4–6 hashtags.
  • Facebook: 4:5, 1080×1350, platform-native caption, 3–4 hashtags.
  • Image count: six. Determined by the Art Director after the outline (see 08-visual-plan.md).

7. Known risks

RiskMitigationOwner
Death-toll figures differ between sources (844 vs 812)Use the official figure, note the Coroner's figure is disputed in the ledgerfact-checker
Competing accounts of the legal outcomeVerify precisely; if unresolved, describe only what is certainfact-checker
Sensitivity of a mass-casualty storyNo corpse or body-recovery imagery; no lingering on sufferingstandards-editor
Period handwriting on one archival photo carries a wrong dateCrop it out of the final frameart-director
Archival scans vary in qualityUnified grade and grain; reject any frame that cannot hold 1080 pximage-producer

8. Constraints

  • Free and public-domain sources only.
  • No paid APIs, subscriptions, or credits. Total spend must remain $0.
  • No posting or publishing. Deliver a package for manual publishing.
  • Respect archive rate limits and terms.

9. Deliverables by stage

See AGENCY.md §3. All artifacts live in content/first-post/.

10. Definition of done

See AGENCY.md §10.

Research — The Ship That Never Left the Dock

Slug: first-post

Journalist: research-journalist

Status: DRAFT → awaiting G2 factual lock

Last updated: 2026-10-19

Claim IDs refer to 03-source-ledger.md.

1. The story in one paragraph

On the morning of July 24, 1915, roughly 2,500 Western Electric employees and their families boarded the excursion steamer Eastland at a wharf on the Chicago River for a company picnic in Michigan City, Indiana. The ship had a documented history of severe listing. New lifeboat requirements, added after the Titanic, had placed additional weight high on an already top-heavy hull. Shortly after 7 a.m., with the gangplank still down and the ship still tied to the dock, the Eastland rolled onto its side. Because the river was only about 20 feet deep and the ship lay only about 20 feet from the wharf, hundreds were able to escape across the exposed hull — but 844 people died, most of them below decks. Prosecutions followed and failed. The ship was raised, sold to the Navy, renamed USS Wilmette, and served into the 1940s.

3. The people

NameRoleVerifiedClaims
The victims (844)Passengers and crew, largely Western Electric employees and their familiesAge and family statistics are documented in the congressional recordC01, C08, C09

We name only people whose involvement is documented in the public record. No one is described as convicted, because no one was.

4. The mechanism

Three factors combined. This is the engineering core of the story.

Design and history. The Eastland was built narrow and fast, which tends to make a hull top-heavy. Its stability was marginal from the start, and it had a documented record of severe listing — in 1904, 1906, and 1912 — before the disaster (C10, C12).

Added top-weight. After the Titanic, the Seamen's Act of 1915 required more lifeboats and rafts. To keep its licensed passenger capacity, the Eastland's operators added boats high on the superstructure. That weight sat above the ship's center of gravity and worsened the very problem that had nearly sunk the ship before (C11).

The morning it happened. Passengers gathered on the side of the ship away from the river as it listed and corrected. When it rolled, the open lower decks and portholes allowed water in quickly, and the ship went onto its side within a short time (C03).

Why so many died, and why so many lived. The Eastland settled into roughly 20 feet of water about 20 feet from the wharf. The shallow water and the proximity of the dock saved hundreds, who climbed out across the exposed hull. It also meant the lower decks flooded within minutes, killing the people trapped there — which is why the death toll was so high despite the ship never leaving the dock (C04, C05, C06).

5. What was done afterward

A coroner's inquest and a grand jury investigated. The grand jury indicted the ship's owners, the captain, the chief engineer, and federal inspectors. The case was moved to Grand Rapids, Michigan, where the defendants were found not guilty in February 1916, and the court refused extradition to Illinois — so no criminal trial was ever held in Chicago. No one was criminally convicted. The civil claims dragged on for years and ended with liability limited to the wreck's salvage value; the families ultimately received no damages (C12). The ship itself was raised on August 14, 1915, sold, and later commissioned as the Navy's USS Wilmette, serving into the 1940s before being scrapped (C13, C14).

6. Disputed / unclear

PointVersion AVersion BHandling
Death toll844 (settled figure)Early press estimates ranged from ~919 to ~1,200 before being correctedUse 844. A discarded "812" circulation must not be repeated.
Crew among the dead2, 3, or 4 depending on source—Do not state a crew figure; describe the dead as "passengers and crew"
Legal outcomeAll verdicts not guilty; no criminal trial in ChicagoA 1933 civil ruling blamed the chief engineer, who had died in 1919State only that the cases ended without a conviction
Titanic comparisonCongressional resolution on civilian passengersGeneral "more than Titanic" claim is falseUse only the narrow, sourced comparison, or drop it
Cause of the initial listPassengers gathering on one sideBallast and engineering factorsDescribe several contributing factors, as the record does

7. What we still do not know

  • The precise second-by-second sequence aboard the lower decks is not recoverable.
  • Sources differ on the exact time the ship rolled; we say "shortly after 7 a.m." to stay safe.
  • The number of crew among the dead is genuinely inconsistent across reputable sources.

8. Quotations available for use

We could not verify any quotation word-for-word from a primary source with a stable citation. No direct quotations will be used. Everything is paraphrased.

9. Notes on sourcing quality

  • NARA and the Library of Congress provide authoritative primary imagery.
  • The congressional record provides the age and family statistics, which is a strong source tier.
  • Popular retellings of the disaster frequently repeat the unfounded "never should have been built"

line and the "more than the Titanic" comparison. Neither will appear unqualified.

  • Wikipedia was used only as a map to better sources, never as a final citation.

Fact-Check — The Ship That Never Left the Dock

Slug: first-post

Checker: fact-checker (independent of research)

Date: 2026-10-19

Gate: G2 — Factual lock

Every claim was re-verified against sources independent of the journalist's notes. Two material errors were found in the draft research and are corrected below.

1. Claim audit

IDClaim as writtenVerdictEvidenceRequired correction
C01844 passengers and crew diedVERIFIEDH.Res. 375; Eastland Disaster Historical SocietyNone. Note that a small number of crew are included in the 844.
C02Coroner's office reported 812UNSUPPORTED / FALSENo primary source supports 812. The coroner convened a jury and ruled cause of death "drowned"; early press figures ranged from ~919 to ~1,200 before the count settled at 844Delete the 812 figure entirely. It does not appear in the caption or the ledger as a competing toll.
C03Capsized while still tied to its wharf, gangplank downVERIFIEDMultiple accounts; the last mooring line parted as the ship went overReword to "still secured to the dock" to stay accurate about the stern line.
C04Shortly after 7 a.m.; 7:28 a.m.VERIFIEDAccounts give 7:28 a.m.; others say about 7:30Use "shortly after 7 a.m." in the caption (safe under both).
C05Roughly 2,500 aboardVERIFIED2,500 is the licensed capacity; ≈2,573 total is also cited"More than 2,500" is defensible; use 2,500.
C06About 20 feet of waterVERIFIEDEDHS: "just twenty feet of water"None.
C07About 20 feet from the wharfVERIFIEDEDHS gives 19 feet for the bow; other sources say 20"About 20 feet" is fine.
C08590 of the dead were under 25VERIFIEDH.Res. 375: "590 of the victims were under the age of 25 including 228 teenagers as well as 58 infants and children"None.
C0922 entire families wiped outVERIFIEDH.Res. 375: "wiped out 22 entire families and left 19 families without parents"Use the resolution's wording.
C10Documented history of severe listingVERIFIEDJuly 17, 1904 (≈3,000 aboard, South Haven); July 1, 1912 (≈25° list, Cleveland)None.
C11Seamen's Act → more lifeboats → added top-weightVERIFIED as a contributing factor onlyAccounts agree the added boats worsened stability, but they were one factor among severalNever present it as the sole cause. Phrase as one of several contributing factors.
C12Indictments; no convictionVERIFIED — and the draft contained two errorsH.Res. 375: "all verdicts returned in the criminal proceedings were 'not guilty"'; defendants found not guilty in February 1916; the court refused extradition, so no criminal trial was held in ChicagoSee §2 below. Delete "Joseph Erickson convicted" and delete "Paul Steinbrecher" entirely.
C13Raised August 14, 1915VERIFIEDMultiple institutional sourcesNone.
C14Sold to Navy, renamed USS Wilmette, served into the 1940s, scrappedVERIFIED (path corrected)Sold at auction December 1915; to the Illinois Naval Reserve November 21, 1917; renamed Wilmette February 20, 1918; decommissioned November 28, 1945; sold for scrap October 31, 1946; scrapping completed 1947Do not say sold directly to the Navy in 1915. Say she was raised, sold, and later became the Navy's Wilmette.
C15Deadliest shipwreck in Great Lakes historyVERIFIEDStandard institutional statementNone.
C16≈3,000 aboard in 1904VERIFIEDInstitutional accountsNone.
C17Helen Repa; Second Regiment Armory morgueVERIFIEDRepa, a Western Electric nurse, organized much of the rescue; the coroner procured the Second Regiment Armory as the central morgueNone.
C18More civilian passengers drowned than on the Titanic or LusitaniaVERIFIED (narrow, congressional)H.Res. 375, 114th Congress: "Whereas more non-crew, civilian passengers drowned on the Eastland than on either the Titanic or the Lusitania"It is an introduced resolution referred to committee, not a passed law. Used only in its narrow form, or not at all.

2. The material errors found

Error 1 — a fabricated name. The draft named "Paul Steinbrecher" as a defendant whose extradition was refused. No person by that name is connected to this case in any source consulted. The six men indicted were Arnold, Hull, Reid, Eckliff, Pedersen, and Erickson. Removed.

Error 2 — wrongly asserting a criminal conviction. The draft repeated the widely circulated claim that chief engineer Joseph Erickson was the only person convicted. This is false. What actually happened:

  • A grand jury indicted the owners, the captain, the chief engineer, and federal inspectors.
  • The case was moved to Grand Rapids, Michigan.
  • In February 1916 the defendants were found not guilty, and the court refused extradition

to Illinois, so no criminal trial was ever held in Chicago.

  • The "Erickson was guilty" story comes from a 1933 civil ruling that attributed the disaster to

his use of the ballast tanks. Erickson had died in 1919. The civil claims ended with liability limited to the wreck's salvage value, and the families ultimately received no damages.

Removed from the draft and the caption.

3. Quotation audit

QuoteAttributed toExact match?Problem
———No quotations are used. None could be verified word-for-word with a stable citation.

4. Number and unit audit

Families wiped out2222Yes
Families without parents1919Yes
Water depth~20 ft20 ftYes
Distance from wharf~20 ft19–20 ftYes
Length265 ft265 ftYes
Aboard~2,5002,500 capacityYes

5. Causation audit

ClaimSource asserts cause?Acceptable as written?Fix
Lifeboat law caused the capsizingNo — it is cited as a contributing factor that worsened stabilityOnly if phrased as one factor among severalUse "made a known problem worse," never "caused"
Shallow water caused the high tollYes — the depth and proximity trapped people below deckYesNone

6. Timeline coherence

Checked. No event is placed before its cause. The 1915 law precedes the 1915 disaster; the 1904 and 1912 listings precede 1915; the raising precedes the Navy service; the criminal acquittal (Feb. 1916) precedes the civil ruling (1933).

7. Superlative audit

ClaimVerified?Qualification needed
Deadliest shipwreck in Great Lakes historyYesNone
More civilian passengers than Titanic/LusitaniaYes, per H.Res. 375Must be the narrow "civilian passengers" form; not used in this caption

8. Lock decision

Status: PASS

All load-bearing claims are VERIFIED. The two disputed items are handled by omission:

  • The 812 figure is removed.
  • No person is named as convicted or prosecuted, and no crew death count is stated.

9. Approved handling language

Visual Sourcing — The Ship That Never Left the Dock

Slug: first-post

Owner: visual-researcher

Gate: G3 — Rights clearance (pending standards-editor)

Date: 2026-10-19

1. Search strategy

We searched Wikimedia Commons, the Library of Congress, the National Archives catalog, and the Newberry Library's Chicago collections for the Eastland.

We filtered for:

  • Authentic period material (1915), not later tourist or modern photographs.
  • Public-domain or no-known-restrictions status, recorded per item.
  • Sufficient resolution to hold 1080 px wide without exceeding a 1.6× upscale.
  • Dignity: no corpse, morgue, or body-recovery imagery.

A note on rate limits: the Commons API returns HTTP 429 under rapid automated requests. We used a descriptive user agent, sequential requests with delays, and a local cache. NARA and the Library of Congress were queried separately.

2. Adopted assets

IDTitleArchiveLicenseRole
01-capsized-naraPhotographic Exhibits of The Eastland (NAID 281841)U.S. National ArchivesUnrestricted / PD-USCover
02-upright-naraPanoramic Photograph of The Eastland (NAID 281840)U.S. National ArchivesUnrestricted / PD-USBefore
05-satterfieldCapsizing of the SS Eastland, as witnessed by SatterfieldThe Tacoma Times, July 27, 1915PD-US (pre-1931)The moment
04-firetug-postcardView of the Eastland taken from a fire tugMax Rigot Selling Co., Chicago, 1915PD-US (pre-1931)Scale
03-rescue-locEastland disaster: rescue operationsLoC, Bain Collection, LCCN 2017658559, LC-USZ62-30114No known restrictionsResponse
07-wreck-panoramaThe wreck of the EastlandLoC, LCCN 2007661460, LC-USZ62-126620, pan.6a04191No known restrictionsClosing plate

Full metadata, credit lines, and alt text are in assets/manifest.json.

Credit corrections applied after independent rights verification

  • The panorama's archive identifier was initially recorded incorrectly. The correct identifiers are

LCCN 2007661460, call number PAN US GEOG – Illinois no. 34, reproduction number LC-USZ62-126620.

  • The rescue photograph is credited to the Bain News Service, not to the collection; the collection

is named for George Grantham Bain.

  • The two NARA items are catalogued as "Photographic Exhibits of The Eastland" and "Panoramic

Photograph of The Eastland." The Commons filenames carry older captions, not the NARA titles.

  • The fire-tug postcard's publisher is the Max Rigot Selling Company, Chicago.

Rights caveat recorded

The two NARA items are tagged PD-USGov on Commons, but they were made by commercial photographers and the defensible public-domain basis is pre-1930 publication, not federal authorship. Under either basis they are free to reproduce in the United States. The 1915 postcard and the Satterfield drawing are public domain in the United States only; both could still be protected in life-plus-70 jurisdictions. That is acceptable because our audience and platforms are US-based, and it is noted here for the record.

3. Rejected assets

AssetReason
06-mourners — Chicago Tribune photographs of mournersConsidered and dropped. The source is a coarse newspaper halftone; at the crop required for 4:5 it shows the print screen badly and frames a grieving woman too tightly. It fails the quality bar and risks being exploitative. The human cost is carried by the caption and by the rescue frame.
Eastland Postcard — "Recovering bodies from the hull"Excluded on dignity grounds. Body-recovery imagery is never used.
EastlandKenosha.jpgOnly 475×381. Far too small for 1080 px.
"Eastland being righted" (port side)Only 478×373. Too small.
CC BY-SA tourist photograph of the siteModern, low value, and a share-alike obligation we do not need.
2013 U.S. Coast Guard ceremonial photographModern and non-documentary.
"Eastland disaster through the eyes of Frank King"A cartoon commentary, not a documentary record.
Chicago Tribune front page scansText-dense and unreadable at 1080 px wide.

4. Gaps and AI-reconstruction decision

The one moment no photograph captures is the capsizing itself — all surviving photographs are after the ship was already over. The 1915 eyewitness newspaper illustration (Satterfield) fills that gap with authentic period material.

No AI reconstruction is required for this post, and none was used. Every image is an authentic 1915 document. Therefore no AI disclosure is needed in the captions.

5. Verification notes

  • Each image was opened and inspected at full size before adoption.
  • The rescue photograph carries period handwriting across the top that includes an incorrect date

("1-24-15"). The final crop removes it so the image cannot be misread.

  • The panorama carries a period caption and a photography-studio stamp. It is published in the

United States in 1915 and is in the public domain.

  • We do not upscale any source beyond 1.6×, and we never colorize.

Narrative Outline — The Ship That Never Left the Dock

Slug: first-post

Owner: story-editor

Gate: G4 — Story approval

Date: 2026-10-19

Structure: hook → context → development → turning point → resolution → ending. Every beat cites the claim IDs it depends on.

Beat 1 — Hook

Purpose: deliver the contradiction in one breath.

The Eastland was still tied to the dock when it killed 844 people.

Two short sentences. A concrete number and an impossible fact. Nothing withheld that the story does not immediately pay off.

Claims: C01, C03

Beat 2 — Context

Purpose: establish why 2,500 people were on a steamship at 7 a.m. on a Saturday.

Western Electric's employees and their families were bound for a company picnic in Michigan City, Indiana. The morning was cool. The gangplank was still down. Nobody had gone anywhere.

Claims: C05, C03, C04

Beat 3 — Development (1): the known flaw

Purpose: show this was not a freak accident.

The Eastland had nearly gone over before — in 1904 with roughly 3,000 aboard, and again in 1912. Its stability was marginal by design.

Claims: C10, C16

Beat 4 — Development (2): the law that made it worse

Purpose: the turn the reader does not expect.

After the Titanic, new safety rules required more lifeboats. To keep its passenger license, the Eastland added boats high on its upper decks. The weight went exactly where the ship could least afford it.

Claims: C11

Beat 5 — Turning point

Purpose: the physical event, plainly told.

Shortly after 7 a.m., the ship rolled onto its side. Water came into the lower decks fast.

Claims: C03, C04

Beat 6 — Why the toll was so high, and why so many lived

Purpose: the cruel geometry that makes this story unique.

The river was about 20 feet deep and the ship lay about 20 feet from the wharf. That shallow, narrow space is why hundreds climbed out alive — and why hundreds below deck had minutes, not hours.

Claims: C06, C07

Beat 7 — Resolution

Purpose: what happened to the dead, the ship, and the people responsible.

844 dead. 590 of them under 25. Twenty-two entire families gone. Indictments followed; the criminal cases ended without anyone held responsible. The ship was raised within weeks, sold to the Navy, renamed USS Wilmette, and served into the 1940s.

Claims: C01, C08, C09, C12, C13, C14

Beat 8 — Ending

Purpose: land the meaning without instructing the reader.

The dock is a short walk from the Loop. The water is 20 feet deep. Most days, nobody looks down.

No call to action. No "follow for more." The final image is a wide panorama of the wreck, and the caption simply stops.

Claims: none (reflection grounded in verified C06, C07)

Section audit

BeatAdds information, context, or feelingKeep
1 HookFact + contradictionYes
2 ContextWho these people wereYes
3 Known flawEstablishes patternYes
4 Law made it worseThe unexpected causeYes
5 Turning pointThe eventYes
6 Geometry of survivalExplains the unique tollYes
7 ResolutionConsequence and aftermathYes
8 EndingMeaningYes

No beat exists only to pad length.

Decisions for copy

  • The Titanic comparison (C18) is available but will not be used in the caption. It is the most

commonly misstated element of this story, and the honest version needs a paragraph of qualification to be fair. Omitting it is stronger than misusing it.

  • No direct quotations, because none could be verified word-for-word with a stable citation.
  • The crew death count is never stated, because sources disagree. The dead are "passengers and crew."

The Eastland was still tied to the dock when it killed 844 people.

Secondary / alt text opener:

844 people died in twenty feet of water, twenty feet from shore.

Rationale: the physical impossibility of the geography is the most durable and least

sensational detail in the story. It works as a standalone line if the primary hook is ever retired.

Pairing check

The cover photograph shows the ship on its side. The hook says it never left the dock. The text and the image each carry a different half of the contradiction — neither is redundant. Scored 4/5 on visual pairing for exactly that reason.

Growth Packaging — The Ship That Never Left the Dock

Slug: first-post

Owner: growth-strategist

Date: 2026-10-19

1. Audience

US adults 25–55 who follow history, engineering failures, and true-story accounts. They are the people who save a post to read later and send it to one specific friend. They respond to concrete detail and they punish exaggeration. The secondary audience is Chicago-area readers, who will recognize the river and the Loop reference and feel a local stake.

2. Search and discovery terms

Words people actually use for this event, and where they appear naturally:

TermWhere it appears
Eastland disasterCaption, first line, hashtag
Chicago River shipwreckBody, first comment
1915 ChicagoDateline on the cover, caption
Great Lakes shipwreckCaption, hashtag
Western Electric picnicBody
ship capsized at dockHook, body

No keyword stuffing. Each term appears once, in a sentence that needs it.

3. Hashtags

Instagram (5):

TagReason
#EastlandDisasterThe exact event name; the highest-intent tag
#ChicagoHistoryStrong local and topical community
#GreatLakesPlaces the story in a region people follow
#MaritimeHistoryReaches the shipwreck and naval-history audience
#ForgottenHistoryThe archive and "things you didn't learn" community

Facebook (4): the same set minus #ForgottenHistory, which performs poorly there.

Rejected: #history, #disaster, #1915 — too broad to route to anyone, and #disaster attracts graphic content we do not want the post adjacent to.

4. Carousel order rationale

Image 1 must earn the swipe on its own. It shows the ship already on its side, which is visually arresting at thumbnail size and does not repeat the headline — the text says "never left the dock" and the image shows the result. Image 2 then answers "what was it?" and the rest deliver the turns. The closing plate gives the reader something to hold: the river today.

5. Share triggers

The lines most likely to be screenshotted or quoted:

  1. "The Eastland was still tied to the dock when it killed 844 people." — the contradiction,

shareable on its own as a fact.

  1. "That shallow, narrow gap is why hundreds climbed across the exposed hull and lived." — the

counterintuitive mechanism; the part people retell.

  1. **"The dock is a short walk from the Loop. The water is 20 feet deep. Most days, nobody looks

down."** — the ending, which carries the "I've walked past this" feeling.

6. Comment prompt

Built into the ending rather than bolted on: readers who know the river will say so, and readers who did not know the event will say that. We do not ask a question. The honest question — how does a disaster of this scale become invisible? — is implied by the last line and left open.

7. Timing

Recommendation: Tuesday or Wednesday, 12:00–1:00 p.m. Eastern, or Sunday 7:00–9:00 p.m. Eastern.

Reasoning: history and long-form accounts perform well in the midday US lunch window and on Sunday evenings, when mobile reading peaks. Avoid Monday mornings, when feed competition is highest and dwell time is lowest. This is a reasoned default, not a measured result for this account, which has no history yet.

8. Viral Readiness Score

CriterionScoreJustification
Hook5"Still tied to the dock" is a concrete contradiction in the first sentence
Curiosity gap4Strong, though the mechanism is explained rather than concealed; we do not withhold
Emotional stakes5844 dead, 590 under 25, 22 families erased; handled without exploitation
Specificity5844, 590, 22, 20 feet, 20 feet, 7 a.m., 1915, named institutions

Saveability5The engineering explanation is worth keeping and re-reading

Standing by the studio rule: this scores the inputs we control, not a prediction of virality.

1. Reply bank

Anticipated commentDrafted response
"I've lived in Chicago my whole life and never knew this.""It's easy to walk past. The site is a few blocks from the Loop, and the river there looks like any other stretch of water."

"The engineer was convicted.""That's a common version, and it isn't accurate. The criminal defendants were found not guilty in 1916 and no trial was held in Chicago. A 1933 civil ruling blamed the engineer, but that was a civil finding after he had already died."
"This is disrespectful.""That's a fair thing to raise. We used only public-domain photographs, avoided any image of the dead, and tried to let the numbers speak rather than dramatize them. If something here reads as disrespectful, tell me which part."
"More people died than on the Titanic.""That's true in one narrow sense — a congressional resolution notes that more civilian passengers drowned on the Eastland than on the Titanic or the Lusitania. In total lives lost, the Titanic was far higher."
"Why does an old disaster matter now?""Because it was an engineering failure that was known in advance and predicted in advance. That part doesn't stay in 1915."

Hostile or dismissive commentNo reply. See moderation rules.
Spam or a sales pitchHide and report. No reply.

2. Moderation rules

ActionApplies to
HideSpam, scams, and comments containing slurs
DeleteTargeted harassment of an identifiable person; anything that identifies a private individual as responsible
ReportThreats, doxxing, coordinated spam
Leave, no replyHostility, bad-faith arguments, "this is boring," off-topic politics
Always replyFactual questions, family connections, good-faith disagreement

We never delete legitimate criticism. We never argue. We never edit someone's comment.

3. Correction protocol

If a posted caption or image contains a material error:

  1. Fix it within 24 hours.
  2. Post a visible note: Correction: followed by what was wrong and what is correct.
  3. Log it in 14-postmortem.md.
  4. If the error is structural (wrong event, wrong death toll, wrong attribution), unpublish and rebuild.

Two known risks to watch: anyone repeating the "812" death toll, and anyone asserting a criminal conviction. Both are addressed in the reply bank.

4. Escalation

  • Factual dispute we cannot resolve → standards-editor, then research-journalist.
  • Rights complaint about an image → standards-editor immediately; the post may be taken down

while it is checked.

  • Media or institutional inquiry → agency-lead.
  • A family member asking us to change something → agency-lead and standards-editor together.

We take it seriously.

5. First 24 hours

A human should watch for:

  • The first hour of comments, when the reply bank's factual answers matter most.
  • Any family connection, which should be answered by a person, not a template.
  • Any correction request, which is handled before anything else.
  • Whether the hook is holding — the ratio of saves to reach in the first three hours.

FINAL REPORT — Cluefolio Studio, Post 001

Delivered: 2026-10-19

Owner: agency-lead

Status: READY FOR HUMAN PUBLISHING

Total cost: $0

1. What was built

A complete, self-contained content agency inside this repository, plus one finished, publication-ready post.

The agency — 18 roles defined in .opencode/agents/, a 11-stage / 6-gate pipeline in AGENCY.md, a 5-file brand system in brand/, 4 reusable templates in templates/, and 3 production scripts in scripts/.

The post — 6 images at 1080×1350, two platform-native captions, alt text for every image, a source ledger with claim IDs, a rights record, a community plan, and QA reports.

Every path below exists on disk. Verified programmatically.

2. The story and the angle

Post 001: "The Ship That Never Left the Dock" — the SS Eastland disaster, Chicago, July 24, 1915. Category: Disasters / Engineering failure.

Angle: A steamship capsized while still secured to its dock, killing 844 people in twenty feet

of water, twenty feet from shore — and no one was ever criminally convicted.

Why this story: it has an irreducible hook in one sentence, genuine engineering substance

(top-weight, stability, and a well-intentioned safety law that made a known flaw worse), an abundant free public-domain visual archive, and it is far less known nationally than its scale warrants.

Why not the others: Triangle Shirtwaist (too familiar), Halifax (heavily covered), Molasses

Flood (thin visuals), Cocoanut Grove (held for a future post). Full scoring in 01-candidates.md.

3. The deliverable package

  images/01-cover.jpg          1080x1350   381 KB
  images/02-upright.jpg        1080x1350   488 KB
  images/03-the-moment.jpg     1080x1350   496 KB
  images/04-the-hull.jpg       1080x1350   648 KB

  images/06-the-wreck.jpg      1080x1350   378 KB

Carousel order: cover → the ship → the moment → the hull → the rescue → the closing plate.

4. How it was produced

The pipeline ran in order, and every gate passed:

GateDecisionDecided by
G1 GreenlightPASS — Eastland selected at 39/40editorial-director
G2 Factual lockPASS after two material correctionsfact-checker (independent)
G3 Rights clearancePASS — all public domain in the USvisual-researcher + standards-editor
G4 Story approvalPASS — 8-beat outlineeditorial-director
G5 ClearanceCLEARED — no vetoesstandards-editor
G6 Sign-offSIGNED OFF — 80/80 checksqa-lead

Two genuine parallel specialist runs were used: an independent fact-checker and a rights auditor, each working from its own sources rather than the research notes.

Revision rounds used: 2 of a maximum 3.

5. Verification — what the fact-check caught

This is the most important section of the report, because G2 changed the post.

Error 1 — a fabricated name. The draft research named "Paul Steinbrecher" as a defendant whose extradition was refused. No such person is connected to the case in any source. Removed.

Error 2 — a false conviction claim. The draft repeated the widely circulated story that chief engineer Joseph Erickson was the only person convicted. This conflates a 1933 civil ruling with criminal guilt. In fact the defendants were found not guilty in February 1916, the court refused extradition to Illinois, and no criminal trial was ever held in Chicago. Erickson had died in 1919. Corrected, and the caption now states only what is certain.

Also corrected: an unsupported "812" death toll removed; the ship's transfer path to the Navy

corrected; the lifeboat law reframed as one contributing factor, not a cause.

Deliberate omissions: the Titanic/Lusitania comparison (true only in a narrow congressional

form that a caption cannot carry honestly) and the crew death count (sources give 2, 3, or 4). No direct quotations are used, because none could be verified word-for-word with a stable citation.

Result: every factual statement in both captions traces to a claim ID in 03-source-ledger.md.

6. Rights and imagery

  • All six images are public domain in the United States or carry a "no known restrictions on

publication" statement from the holding institution.

  • No AI was used anywhere. Every image is an authentic 1904–1915 document, so no AI disclosure

is required.

  • Imagery was verified against catalog records, not filenames. The rights audit corrected the

panorama's archive identifiers (the correct ones are LCCN 2007661460 and LC-USZ62-126620), the Bain News Service creator credit, the two NARA catalog titles, and the postcard publisher.

  • Dignity: the body-recovery postcard and the mourning-photograph frame were both sourced and

deliberately rejected. No image of the dead is used.

  • Rights caveat recorded: the 1915 postcard and the Satterfield drawing are public domain in the

US only and may still be protected in life-plus-70 jurisdictions. Acceptable for a US audience and US platforms.

7. Quality assurance

python scripts/validate_post.py --slug first-post → 80/80 checks passed, SIGNED OFF.

Every image was opened at full size and inspected. Six defects were found and fixed during inspection, including an illegible cover tag, a period photograph carrying an incorrect date in its own handwriting, and an inaccurate statement on the closing plate.

Viral Readiness Score: 37/40. Exceeds the 32 publish floor and the 36 flagship bar. The score measures inputs we control, not a prediction of virality.

8. Cost and resources

Total spend: $0. No paid APIs, no subscriptions, no credits, no purchases. Free models only.

resources/resource-register.md records four buckets: what was already available and reusable, what was verified and adopted (Wikimedia Commons, NARA, LoC, Pillow, numpy), what was useful but inaccessible (Pollinations now returns HTTP 402; no image API keys; no discrete GPU for local diffusion), and what was investigated and rejected — including paid generation, AI upscaling of archival scans, scraping social platforms, and building a database the project does not need.

9. Known limits and honest caveats

  1. The post is not published. Nothing was posted, scheduled, or boosted. A human must publish it.
  2. No performance data exists, so 14-postmortem.md is deliberately empty rather than estimated.
  3. Pre-1930 dating is the defensible public-domain basis for the two NARA images, not federal

authorship — both are fine in the US.

  1. Two images are US-only public domain and would need review before use in other markets.
  2. Some archival scans are soft or coarse (the fire-tug postcard; the rescue aerial). They are

authentic and readable, but they are not high-fidelity photographs.

  1. The Facebook and Instagram captions share one narrative, as required, but are written

separately and are not copies of each other.

10. What to do next

To publish: upload images/01–06 in order, paste captions/instagram.md and

captions/facebook.md, attach the matching alt text from captions/alt-text.md to each image, and put the source list in the Instagram first comment. Recommended window: Tuesday or Wednesday, 12:00–13:00 ET, or Sunday 19:00–21:00 ET.

To operate the agency for Post 002: create content/<slug>/, write the brief from

templates/brief.md, run the pipeline, and do not start writing until G2 passes. The three scripts and the templates are reusable unchanged.

Immediate improvements this post proved necessary:

  • Verify every archive identifier against the holding institution. Never write one from memory.
  • Decide on a candidate image at sourcing time. Do not carry an unused asset into the manifest

as an afterthought.
